podcast.title: Transistor Radio Entry (1955)
podcast.body: Originally named Tokyo Telecommunications and headed by Masaru Ibuka, the company renamed itself Sony and entered the transistor radio market in August 1955. Their initial unit cost $40, which later dropped to $25, and by 1962, a portable transistor radio from Sony could be purchased for about $15, significantly contributing to the format's affordability and widespread adoption. `"His company, Tokyo Telecommunications, set about building a radio called the TR-55. Then the company was renamed Sony, and it jumped into the fight in August 1955 with a unit that cost $40."`

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 1

podcast.title: Cassette Standardization (1965)
podcast.body: Sony played a crucial role in the global standardization of the compact cassette. Philips made a strategic licensing deal with Sony in 1965, granting them free rights to use the Philips design. With the backing of this "Japanese Giant," the Philips cassette design was adopted as the worldwide standard, leading to over 100 billion cassettes entering the marketplace over subsequent decades. `"It wasn't until Philips made a licensing deal with Sony in 1965, giving them the right to use the design for free, that things really began to take off. With support from the Japanese Giants, the Philips design was standardized for the planet, and over the decades more than 100 billion cassettes entered the marketplace."`

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 1

podcast.title: Licensing of CD Technology (After 1970)
podcast.body: A few years after Jim Russell secured the first patent for his optical recording and playback device in 1970 (which essentially was the first compact disk), Sony, in partnership with Phillips, acquired licenses to further develop this nascent technology into a marketable consumer product. "A few years later, Sony and Phillips purchased the licenses to develop the technology into consumer product."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Inventors

podcast.title: Pressure for Cassette Patent Liberation (1971)
podcast.body: Sony played a significant role in pressuring Philips to release its patent for the cassette tape in 1971. This liberation was critical, as it enabled Sony to manufacture and innovate with cassette tapes, which was a prerequisite for its future developments in portable audio. "sobre todo para que Sony la presionaba, para que Sony pudiese manejar también en la cinta de cassette."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: ESPECIAL FORMATOS: EL CASSETTE

podcast.title: VCR US Supreme Court Ruling (1976)
podcast.body: A landmark 1976 US Supreme Court ruling affirmed the legality of devices such as Sony's VCRs. This decision established that such technologies were permissible because they enabled private copying of copyrighted material for personal use, setting a crucial precedent for future legal battles involving recording and playback devices. "Diamond Multimedia won the case based on a 1976 US Supreme Court ruling that made it okay for Sony to sell VCRs. That decision said that such devices were legal because they allowed for private copying of material, copying of material for private use."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 2

podcast.title: Digital Recording and Optical Disk Development (1977-1978)
podcast.body: In Japan, Sony was actively developing digital recording machines and first showcased a 30-centimeter optical disk (the same diameter as a vinyl LP) in September 1977, capable of holding 60 minutes of music. A year later, they advanced this to a disk holding up to 150 minutes, still at 30 centimeters. "Meanwhile, in Japan, Sony was working on digital recording machines and first demonstrated an optical disk that was 30 centimeters in diameter. So the same diameter as a vinyl LP, one foot. This was September 1977."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rise and Fall of the CD

podcast.title: CD Development Collaboration (1979)
podcast.body: Sony, having a head start in digital storage technology, teamed up with Philips in 1979 to develop the compact disk. Sony contributed all its knowledge from prior work, including demonstrations of optical disks in 1977 and 1978 that could hold varying lengths of music. The collaboration shared research costs and aimed to establish proper standards for the new music storage format. `"Meanwhile, Sony, which had a head start in digital storage technology, contributed everything that they knew."`

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 1

podcast.title: Collaboration with Philips on CD Standards (1979)
podcast.body: Sony teamed up with Philips in 1979 after both companies realized they were working toward the same goal for a new music storage format. This collaboration involved splitting research costs, sharing knowledge, and establishing the proper standards, resulting in the "Red Book CDDA standard." "In 1979, when Sony and Phillips realized that they were working towards the same goal, the companies teamed up to split the costs of research, to share knowledge, and to come up with all the proper standards for making this new music storage format."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rise and Fall of the CD

podcast.title: Compact Disk Development Partnership (1979)
podcast.body: Sony joined Phillips in 1979 to collaborate on the development of the compact disk technology. Their involvement was instrumental in setting a worldwide standard for CDs, including specifications for material (polycarbonate), diameter (120 millimeters), laser reading direction (inside-out), and maximum length (74 minutes), reputedly to accommodate the Sony chairman's favorite Beethoven symphony. "In 1979 Sony gets on board to help out with development."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8

podcast.title: Contribution to Red Book CDDA Standard (1979)
podcast.body: Sony, having a head start in digital storage technology, contributed its expertise to the creation of the Red Book CDDA standard. This collection of specifications, designed in 1979, remains the basis for manufacturing compact discs globally today. "Meanwhile, Sony, which had a head start in digital storage technology, contributed what they knew. The result was something known as the Red Book CDDA standard, which is a collection of specifications that are still used to make compact discs everywhere on the planet today."

podcast.title: Introduction of the Walkman (1979)
podcast.body: In 1979, Sony began selling the Walkman, a portable cassette player designed to be worn on a belt and used with headphones. This product quickly became a commercial success but also ignited a patent dispute with Andreas Pavel, who had conceived a similar device years earlier. "It was 1979. Sony started selling something called the Walkman."

srcs.episode: The Inventors

podcast.title: Introduction of the Walkman (1979)
podcast.body: In 1979, Sony revolutionized the music industry with the introduction of the Walkman, the first truly portable device designed for listening to cassette tapes. This invention fundamentally transformed music consumption by enabling personal, on-the-go audio experiences, marking a pivotal moment in musical culture. "el grandísimo invento que cambiaría la cultura musical para siempre fue cuando en 1979 Sony presenta el Waltman, el primera para toportátil para escuchar casets."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: ESPECIAL FORMATOS: EL CASSETTE

podcast.title: Walkman (1979) - Portable Cassette Player
podcast.body: Sony launched the Walkman on July 1, 1979, as a modification of their "Pressman" audio recorder for journalists. Requested by Sony head Masaru Ibuka for long flights, the original TPS-LP2 model was small, light, and came with high-quality headphones. It uniquely featured two headphone jacks, reflecting an initial belief that users wouldn't want complete isolation. Initially branded as Soundabout, Stowaway, or Freestyle in various regions, it was eventually standardized globally as the Walkman. Priced at $150 in 1979 (nearly $600 today), Sony projected monthly sales of 5,000 units but sold 30,000 in its first 60 days, fundamentally changing portable music and boosting cassette sales. `"So imagine his surprise. When on July 1st, 1979, Sony started selling something called the Walkman."`

podcast.title: Commercial Launch of the Compact Disc (1980)
podcast.body: Sony and Philips jointly presented the new music reproduction system, the Compact Disc, commercially in 1980. They introduced it with a complex licensing system designed to allow any company to utilize the technology and develop CD systems. "El nacimiento comercial del disco compacto es en 1980 cuando Sony y Philips a la vez presentan este nuevo sistema de reproducción de música."

podcast.title: First CD Machine - CDP-101 (1982)
podcast.body: By late 1982, the compact disk technology was ready, and Sony released the first CD player, the CDP-101. This machine went on sale for about $700. It offered instant track skipping, a revolutionary feature at the time, providing direct access to any song on the disk without fast-forwarding or rewinding. `"By late 1982, the technology was ready. And the first machine, the Sony CDP-101, went on sale for about 700 bucks."`

podcast.title: First Compact Disc Player, CDP 101 (October 1, 1982)
podcast.body: Sony introduced the world's first compact disc player, the CDP 101, on the afternoon of October 1, 1982. The "CDP" stands for Compact Disk Player, and "101" is binary for the number 5, indicating it was considered a mid-range model in Sony's anticipated future lineup. "Back on the afternoon of October 1st, 1982, Sony introduced a new home stereo gizmo. It was the world's first compact display. They called it the CDP 101."

podcast.title: Japanese CD Market Launch (October 1, 1982)
podcast.body: On October 1, 1982, Sony Japan initiated a significant market launch by issuing 50 compact disc titles simultaneously. "On October 1, 1982, Sony Japan issued 50 titles all at once."

podcast.title: First Car CD Player (1984)
podcast.body: Sony introduced a car CD player in 1984, almost concurrently with Pioneer's CDX-1. This marked Sony's early entry into providing in-car compact disc playback capabilities, catering to the growing demand for digital audio on the go. `"Sony had one out at almost exactly the same time."`

podcast.title: First US CD Manufacturing Plant (October 1984)
podcast.body: Sony opened the first US-based compact disc manufacturing plant in Terre Haute, Indiana, in October 1984. The first CD produced at this facility was Bruce Springsteen's "Born in the USA." "Another milestone was the opening of the first US-based manufacturing plant. A Sony facility went online in Tarot Hote, Indiana, in October 1984."

podcast.title: Patent Dispute and Settlement with Pavel (1986, 2003)
podcast.body: Sony engaged in negotiations with Andreas Pavel over alleged violations of his patent related to the personal music player concept. An initial agreement in 1986 addressed Walkman sales only in Germany, while attempts at a similar settlement in the UK were unsuccessful and costly for Pavel. However, in 2003, Sony and Pavel reached an out-of-court settlement, rumored to include $10 million in cash and a share of royalties from certain Walkman models. "He began to negotiate with Sony over what he considered to be violations of his patent."

"That was deliberate on the part of Carey and Sony music at the time."

podcast.title: London Headquarters Knife Fight (2018)
podcast.body: In November 2018, the headquarters of Sony Music in London, England, was stormed by police, leading to the evacuation of the building and the closure of surrounding streets. The incident stemmed from a fight between two chefs in the catering department, who attacked each other with knives, resulting in injuries but no fatalities. "In November 2018, police stormed the headquarters of Sony Music in London, England."

podcast.title: "Magic Trick" Chart Strategy
podcast.body: Sony Music pioneered a "magic trick" strategy in the mid-1990s to achieve number one debuts, particularly with Michael Jackson's "Scream" and "You Are Not Alone," and Mariah Carey's "Fantasy." This involved pre-hyping songs to radio for an extended period (up to two months) before releasing them as retail singles, thus exploiting Billboard's rule that songs were ineligible until for sale. Upon release, massive first-week sales combined with pre-existing strong airplay guaranteed instant number one positions. "Sony Music, Michael Jackson's label, had been promoting screen to pop radio stations for about a month when the single arrived in stores."

podcast.body: Concurrent with Mini Disk development, Sony also worked on Digital Audio Tape (DAT). However, the DAT format encountered numerous issues and never became a widespread consumer product, primarily because the recorded music industry insisted on extensive copy protection measures, which made DAT machines too expensive and largely impractical for the general public. "Part of the delay was because Sony was also working on digital audio tape or date at the same time. But that format ran into a ton of problems and never really became a consumer thing."

"Sony's Discmin was the CD version of the Walkman. Nice idea, but it was bigger than a portable cassette player. It was hard to drag around a wallet of CDs with you. podcast.title: Mini Disk Licensing to Other Manufacturers
podcast.body: Sony licensed its Mini Disk technology to several other electronics manufacturers, including Alpine, Clarion, Blaupunkt, JVC, Kenwood, Panasonic, and Pioneer, expanding the format's reach in the market. "And as with the CD, the technology was licensed to other manufacturers like Alpine, Clarion, Blaupunk, JBC, Kenwood, Panasonic, Pioneer, and others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 2

podcast.title: Mini Disk Market Performance and Discontinuation
podcast.body: The Mini Disk format achieved considerable success in Japan and Europe but did not gain significant traction in North America, ultimately being viewed as a disappointment despite its practical uses, such as recording interviews in the audio business. Sony supported the Mini Disk until September 2011, with the last players being phased out by early 2013, having sold only about 22 million units worldwide, a stark contrast to the 350 million Sony Walkmans sold. "The format did great in Japan and Europe. North America? Not so much. Some of us used mini disks in the audio business. They were really handy for recording interviews. But overall, the mini disk was a disappointment. However, there was a period of time when you could walk into a good sized record store and find a small display filled with pre-recorded mini disks. Sony stuck with the mini disk until September 2011. And last players were gone by sometime in early 2013. And if you missed the mini disk boat, don't worry. Only about 22 million units were sold worldwide. And remember that the Sony Walkman sold 350 million."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 2

podcast.title: One of Three Major Labels
podcast.body: Sony is identified as one of the three major recorded music companies. "their number has been whittled down to just three companies, the Universal, the biggest, Sony and Warner music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: One of Three Major Labels (Present Day)
podcast.body: Sony is identified as one of the three major multinational record labels in the present day, along with Universal and Warner, controlling numerous subsidiary labels. "Today, we're down to just three. Universal, Sony and Warner and all their subsidiary labels, and there were dozens and dozens of those."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Post-Contract Mixtape Release
podcast.body: PXXR GANG released a free mixtape just days after "Los Pobres" came out, an act considered unthinkable if they had a strict exclusivity contract with Sony. "A los pocos días lanzaron un mixtape gratuito, algo intensable si hubiese firmado un contrato de exclusividad con ellos."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: La salvaje historia del TRAP ESPAÑOL (2013-2026)

podcast.title: Press Play (Failed Online Music Store)
podcast.body: Sony was a joint venture partner in "Press Play," one of two early online music stores created by major labels in an attempt to sell digital files. This service was difficult to use, came with restrictions, and included complicated digital rights management (DRM) safeguards. It was a disaster, lasting only about two years before being shuttered in March 2003. "There was Press Play, which was a joint venture between Universal and Sony."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 10: (10-1)

podcast.title: Promotional Power for Oasis
podcast.body: Sony Music's acquisition of Creation Records coincided with Oasis's contract signing, providing the band with immense promotional potential and financial backing from a major multinational corporation from the very beginning. This significantly contributed to Oasis's rapid and widespread success. "el lanzamiento de oasis tiene detrás todo ese potencial y toda esa promoción más iba hacia Sony Music por detrás."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: OASIS: Pilares del Brit Pop

podcast.title: Proprietary ATRAC Codec
podcast.body: Some of Sony's digital music players utilized a proprietary audio codec known as ATRAC, instead of the more widely adopted MP3 format. This choice led to compatibility issues and contributed to a fragmented market landscape before the advent of the iPod. "Sony had a couple of digital players, but they used a proprietary codec known as ATRAC, not MP3s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 2

podcast.title: Quadraphonic Record Development (1970s)
podcast.body: Sony was among several prominent companies, including Columbia Records and EMI, that actively worked on developing methods to encode four audio channels onto a single vinyl record groove for quadraphonic sound. They eventually agreed upon the SQ system as a common standard. "A lot of companies worked on this, including Sony, Columbia Records, and EMI."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of Stereo: Part 2

podcast.title: Retains John Lennon's Songs
podcast.body: Sony will retain ownership of John Lennon's songs until 70 years after his death (after 2050), despite Paul McCartney regaining control of his own works. "John Lennon's songs, however, will remain with Sony until 70 years after his death. None of his errors will see the benefit of that money until sometime after 2050."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Buying Catalogues - A Primer

podcast.title: Rootkit Scandal
podcast.body: Sony was implicated in a major controversy involving the installation of rootkit malware on customers' computers when they ripped CDs to their systems. This incident contributed to widespread public distrust of copy protection software, which then affected other labels, including Capitol Records and the Beastie Boys. "Sony was busted for this."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Remembering the Beastie Boys Part 2

podcast.title: Scooping Up Catalogs
podcast.body: Sony is listed among the publishing arms of major labels that are actively acquiring catalogs, especially from artists who have been their long-time signings. "Then you add in the publishing arms of labels like Universal and Sony and Warner, who were also scooping up catalogues, usually of artists who have been their signings for years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Buying Catalogues - A Primer

podcast.title: Strategic Licensing for CD Standardization
podcast.body: Learning from Philips' slow-evolving cassette patent and the video format wars (VHS vs. Beta), Sony and Philips joined forces to facilitate easy development for other companies. This strategy aimed to establish the Compact Disc as an industry standard quickly. "Sony y Philips decidieron sumar fuerzas para desarrollar de manera conjunta y sobre todo facilitar un montón el desarrollo a todas las otras empresas para convertir el disco compacto en un estandar de la industria."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: ESPECIAL FORMATOS: El CD

podcast.title: Strategy of Independent Label Acquisition
podcast.body: To address its lack of a major star, Sony's strategy involved acquiring several independent record labels in the early 1990s, including Creation Records. "una de las estrategias que terminaron son los recursos comprando varias discográficas independientes y precisamente vale o seguro. Una de esas discográficas independientes que compra Sony Records a primeros de los 90 es Crisson Records."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: El BRIT POP como negocio discográfico

podcast.title: Vevo Joint Venture Partner
podcast.body: Sony was a key partner in the joint venture that created Vevo, which launched on December 8, 2009. As one of the four major record labels, Sony collaborated to establish a controlled platform for music videos, aiming to attract high-value advertisers and offer premium content. "Vivo, a joint venture between the four major record labels at the time, Universal, Sony, Warner and EMI."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 2

podcast.title: Walkman Advertisement
podcast.body: An advertisement for the Sony Walkman highlighted its compact size, stereo cassette playback, and "truly incredible sound," promising users a profound musical experience and a new perspective on the world. `"The Sony Walkman is a tiny stereo cassette player with truly incredible sound. You're really feeling the music, you're really feeling the music. Put on a Walkman and see the world in a whole new light. Sony Walkman from Sony, the one and only."`
